name: Ironveil PMC Freecontract Assault Kit
description: Stripped-back matte-black and raw-iron grey mixed-source armor — ceramic plates from three different manufacturers, ballistic-weave fatigues patched and re-patched, marked only by a stenciled iron-veil mask logo in flat white on the left pauldron and helmet side. The helmet is a salvaged-military full-face shell with aftermarket thermal optics and a cracked but functional blast visor, held together with bonding resin and pride. Load rig is heavy-duty third-party webbing carrying whatever the current contract requires — the pouches are worn, re-sewn, and unlabeled. Boots are mismatched composite-toe tactical, both functional, neither matching, both resoled at least twice.
functionality: Modular load configuration adaptable to any contract type, aftermarket thermal overlay, and durable enough to survive being field-repaired indefinitely.
what_it_says: No corp owns them, no corp protects them — they get the job done and they've survived long enough to prove it.
worn_by: former corpsec who burned their contracts
manufacturer: Ironveil PMC (independent, no fixed manufacturer — sourced per operative)
story_hooks: The ceramic plate over one operative's heart is stamped with a Stahl-Koenig IronGuard serial number — someone took it off a body, and the original owner's name is still written inside in marker.
Ironveil just took a contract that puts them directly opposite a Halcyon Dynamics detail — and two of the Ironveil operators used to wear gold-and-navy.
related_entities: Arcturus Defense Solutions IronVeil Automaton Command Interf

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian combat silhouette — broad-shouldered, angular, deliberately unglamorous. The wearer appears built for function over form, with layered armor plates breaking the body's lines into geometric planes. The overall impression is industrial and worn, suggesting repeated field deployment rather than parade ground polish.
physical_description.fit: Compression-fitted undersuit with strategic loose panels over joints; armor plates sit flush against the torso in a modular three-plate configuration. Fatigues are tailored for movement and load-bearing, with intentional room at the hips and thighs for gear and weapon access. Deliberately anti-form-fitting.
physical_description.primary_material: Ceramic composite armor plates (mixed-source, visible seams and color variation), ballistic-weave ripstop fatigues (synthetic blend, treated for water and flame), heavy-duty synthetic webbing load rig, salvaged military polymer helmet shell, vulcanized composite-toe boot construction
physical_description.texture: Matte surfaces throughout — ceramic plates have slight micro-roughness from manufacturing variation, ballistic weave shows slight nap and visible stitching, webbing is worn smooth in high-friction areas with fraying at edges, helmet shell has stress fractures visible under the thermal optics mount, visor has spider-web cracking
physical_description.color_scheme: Matte black as primary (fatigues, webbing, undersuit); raw iron grey on ceramic plates (varied tone due to mixed sourcing); flat white stenciled Ironveil mask logo (left pauldron and helmet); gunmetal grey on exposed hardware and webbing anchors; khaki/tan on boot soles (worn and discolored)
physical_description.closures: Heavy-duty magnetic snaps and friction-fit connectors on armor plates; traditional mil-spec velcro on load-bearing webbing; mechanical chin strap on helmet (para-cord rewrapped); side-zip on left leg fatigues; lace-up boots with metal eyelets (one re-punched)
distinctive_features: Stenciled white Ironveil mask logo — stark, minimal, almost medieval in aesthetic
Three-plate asymmetrical ceramic chest configuration suggesting field-improvised repairs
Salvaged military helmet with aftermarket thermal optics (visible mounting seams)
Cracked blast visor held in place with bonding resin (visible clouding and spider fractures)
Heavy-duty third-party webbing with unlabeled worn pouches — some re-sewn with contrasting thread
Mismatched composite-toe boots (different manufacturers, different sole conditions, both re-soled at least twice with visible repair ridges)
Visible stress points where webbing anchors to plates — small tears re-bound with ballistic tape
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 4-5 operative — not corpo-issued (mixed sourcing rules out government/corporate uniformity), too functional for civilian wear, too broken-in for Tier 2-3 contractors who can afford fresh kits
physical_description.cultural_context: Independent PMC operative, likely freelance or with small cell; suggests lengthy contract history (multiple repair cycles), comfort with salvaged/mixed-source equipment, prioritizes reliability over aesthetics. The wearer is seasoned enough to not care about matching gear, experienced enough to keep it functional anyway.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field-worn, patched, weathered. Ceramic plates show scuffing. Fatigues have visible seam repairs (contrasting thread on left leg, right sleeve cuff re-hemmed). Load rig webbing shows shine in high-contact areas. Helmet visor clouding and resin repair visible. Boots are thoroughly resoled with varying material densities. No pristine elements — everything has been used hard and maintained through necessity rather than pride.
